heading: Deployment topology
body: The platform runs across two cloud regions in an active and standby arrangement. Customer traffic enters through a regional load balancer, passes the gateway tier, and reaches a small group of application services running on a shared container cluster. Background work runs on a separate worker pool, which scales on queue depth and can be drained on its own during maintenance. Stateful systems sit in a private network zone that application hosts reach through connection poolers and not directly. Each region holds its own object storage and its own cache, while the primary database replicates from the active region to the standby one. Failover between regions is a manual decision made by the incident lead, and it gets rehearsed during scheduled game days. This library ships inside several of those application services as a plain dependency, with no deployment of its own and no process to operate anywhere in this picture.

heading: Data retention
body: Data on the wider platform falls into three retention classes. Operational records, meaning anything a customer can see or change, stay in the primary database for as long as the account is active and for a fixed grace period after it closes. Event data flows into the warehouse and ages out on a rolling schedule set by the data governance group, with older rows kept only in aggregate. Raw request logs go first of all; they sit in cold object storage for a few weeks and then a lifecycle rule removes them. Deletion requests from customers go through a central queue that fans out to each system holding personal data, and the legal team keeps the record of completion. Backups follow their own clock and are not searched to satisfy individual requests. Anyone adding a new data store assigns it to one of these classes during design review.

heading: Incident history
body: A few past incidents still shape how the platform is run. The longest outage began with a certificate that expired on an internal load balancer over a holiday weekend, and it led to the automated renewal job and the expiry dashboard the infrastructure group now watches. Another came from a cache cluster failover that sent every read to the primary database at once; the connection poolers were added in the weeks after that. A quieter but more expensive event involved a misconfigured lifecycle rule that removed archived exports from object storage before anyone noticed, which is why storage policies now pass through a second person. Postmortems from all of these sit in the operations wiki, and they are written without assigning blame. Most of them share a pattern: a slow change in one layer met an assumption in another, and nobody owned the seam between the two.

heading: Glossary
body: A few words carry a specific meaning across the platform. A tenant is one paying organization, and everything stored belongs to exactly one tenant. A workspace is a subdivision inside a tenant, usually matching a site or department. A member is a licensed person within a tenant, whether or not they have ever signed in. The control plane refers to the services that configure tenants, while the data plane refers to the ones that serve their daily traffic. A cell is a group of tenants pinned to the same database and cache, and moving a tenant between cells is called rehoming. The gateway is the public entry tier, distinct from the edge, which means the content delivery layer in front of it. A rollout is any gradual change of running software, and a cutover is the moment traffic moves from an old system to a new one. To drain a host means stopping new work on it while letting current work finish.

heading: Service ownership
body: Ownership is organized around a handful of groups rather than individual services. The infrastructure group runs the container cluster, networking, the load balancers and the shared databases. The identity group holds sign-in, permissions and tenant configuration. The billing group owns invoicing, payment integrations and the statements customers download. A data group looks after the warehouse, the tracking plan and the pipelines feeding them. Product teams own the application services they build, including the alerts those services produce and the rotation that answers them. Every service has a single named owning group in the service catalog, and shared components without a clear owner default to the infrastructure group until someone claims them. When an issue crosses two groups, the group seeing customer impact leads the response and pulls in the others. Libraries like this one sit with whichever team last needed them, and they are not part of any rotation.

heading: Observability
body: Every service on the platform sends metrics, structured logs and traces to a shared collector, which forwards them to separate long-term stores. Dashboards are grouped by user journey rather than by service, since a customer cares about signing in or downloading a statement and not about which host handled it. Alerts fire on symptoms that a customer would notice, such as failed sign-ins or stalled background queues, and cause-based signals stay on dashboards for people to read during an investigation. Trace context travels across service calls and the event bus, which lets an on-call engineer follow one request from the gateway through to the database. Log sampling is applied at the collector, with longer retention for anything marked as an audit event. Synthetic probes run from outside the network and act as the last line of detection when internal signals go quiet. A library without its own process shows up here only through the services that embed it.

heading: Environments and access
body: There are three long-lived environments: sandbox, staging and production. Sandbox is open to any engineer and gets rebuilt from scratch on a regular schedule, so nothing valuable stays there for long. Staging mirrors the production topology at a smaller scale and holds anonymized copies of real data. Production access is brokered: an engineer requests a short-lived role through the access portal, states a reason, and the grant expires by itself at the end of the session. Service credentials are stored in a central secrets manager and rotated on a schedule owned by the infrastructure group. Human access to customer data carries an extra approval and shows up in a weekly audit review by the security team. Network rules keep the three environments apart, and traffic between them is limited to the anonymization job that refreshes staging. New contractors start with sandbox access only and move up once their onboarding checklist is complete.

heading: How data moves
body: Customer data reaches the platform by three routes: the web application, scheduled file uploads from customer systems, and a partner integration API. All three pass through the gateway, which authenticates the caller and attaches the tenant identifier before anything else happens. Uploaded files sit in a quarantine bucket until a scanner clears them, after which a background worker parses them and writes the results to the primary database. Changes to operational records are published on the event bus, where the search indexer, the notification service and the warehouse loader each consume them at their own pace. Customer-facing exports travel the opposite way, assembled by a worker and handed out through short-lived download links. Nothing leaves the private network zone without passing the gateway or the outbound proxy, and the security team reviews any new path before it opens. Libraries embedded in the workers see only the values handed to them.
